title: remembrance
hook: remembrance; the name on the breath
tomorrow: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mool Mantar, line two. Nirbhau, nirvair. Without fear, without hate. Did one tense conversation go a little differently? Day seven, the end of your first week.

You walk into a room and forget why you came in. You set your keys down and two minutes later they're gone. You meet someone at a party and their name falls out of your head before they've finished saying it. We forget all day long. Mostly it's harmless. But there's a deeper kind of forgetting too: whole days when you never once remember what matters to you, what you're grateful for, what you believe is real. You just get carried along. Sikhs have a word for the opposite of that, and a surprisingly physical way of doing it. Today, the word that ties this first week together.
screen: `WHY DID I COME IN HERE?` → `WHOLE DAYS OF FORGETTING.` → `THE OPPOSITE HAS A WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is simran. Remembrance, calling to mind. In Sikh practice it means remembering God, and especially remembering the name, the naam you met on day five, the whole presence of what is real. How do you remember something all day long? You tie it to something you do all day long anyway. You breathe. So one of the simplest forms of simran is this: breathe in with Wahe, breathe out with guru. The word from day two, riding on the breath. Some Sikhs do it sitting still in the early morning, some with a string of prayer beads, some while they drive, cook or fall asleep. It can be sung aloud with a whole room, or said silently, with no one around you any the wiser. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, wrote a long hymn called Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, and it keeps circling back to simran: remember, and remember, and remember, and find peace; remembering the name, he says, pain and worry fall away. And notice how this first week fits together. Seva, serving with your hands. Waheguru, the name that is a cry of wonder. Nanak, who kept asking what things were for. Ik Onkar, there is one. The root verse: truth is the name, without fear, without hate. Simran is how all of that stays with you after the lesson ends. Not by thinking harder. By remembering, gently, again and again, on the breath.
screen: `SIMRAN — REMEMBRANCE.` · `WAHE IN. GURU OUT.` · `REMEMBER, AND FIND PEACE.` · `HOW THE WEEK STAYS WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THE NAME ON THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. If you'd like to try simran in one way Sikhs teach it: breathe in slowly and let the word Wahe ride in with it. Breathe out and let guru ride out. Three times. If that word isn't yours, just remember one thing on each inhale that you don't want to forget today.
Simran. Remembrance: calling God, the name, to mind, again and again, often on the breath. Seventh word. One week.
Your line: remember on the inhale. Today, three times, at a red light, a kettle, a doorway, take one breath and remember. Next week: the kitchen, the work, the sharing. Day seven.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERYONE ON THE FLOOR, EVERYONE THE SAME MEAL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating Waheguru, silently or aloud, often in the early morning, sometimes with prayer beads, and also by singing the scripture together in the gurdwara.

fork.setup: you want to remember something all day long, without carrying a notebook. what do you tie it to?
options: an alarm on your phone every hour.
your breath, which goes with you everywhere.
a note stuck to the fridge.
fork.reveal: simran rides on the breath: Wahe in, guru out. you breathe all day anyway.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: remembrance, calling to mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: some kind of meditation.
what it means: remembrance: calling God and the name to mind, again and again, often on the breath.
what a scholar hears: simran is related to the Sanskrit smarana, remembering. Guru Arjan's Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, returns to it again and again.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262 onward (Sukhmani Sahib of Guru Arjan, on simran)

notes: Sukhmani Sahib paraphrased ('remember, and remember, and remember, and find peace'; 'pain and worry fall away'), from its opening ashtpadi at Ang 262. Confirm the paraphrase and Ang.
Breath practice (Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath) is a common teaching; some teach other patterns. Confirm.
